💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Best espresso machines for home must thread a delicate needle.
  • In a recent development, I tend to favor devices that let technology do much of the work and don’t make you join a cult of engineers before your first cup.
  • It has been revealed that but I know not everyone wants to also buy a good coffee grinder or spend four figures for their morning cup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Best espresso machines for home must thread a delicate needle. Espresso is forceful and finicky, and a little intimidating, and yet so essential that astronauts might take it into orbit. A home espresso machine remains the most intense and expensive device I regularly operate before my first cup of coffee.

In a recent development, I tend to favor devices that let technology do much of the work and don’t make you join a cult of engineers before your first cup. And so my top-rated espresso machine, the Fellow Series 1, earned its place on WIRED’s counter by combining ease of use with a solid build, consistent temperature, and rare control over pressure—an industry-beating mix of nerdiness and hand-holding friendliness. For a more classic, all-analog build, we offer the compact, stylish Diletta Mio.

It has been revealed that but I know not everyone wants to also buy a good coffee grinder or spend four figures for their morning cup. For those who want milk-based drinks and a built-in grinder, I recommend the top-selling Breville Barista Express as the Goldilocks machine balancing performance and cost. For an entry-level device, I pretty much always recommend the straight-ahead Breville Bambino, among the lowest-cost machines with PID-controlled temperature.

Note that this guide mostly covers classic, hands-on espresso machines with portafilters. We do also include the De'Longhi Rivelia, our top pick among super-automatic espresso machines that require little more than a button press. For a guide that focuses on easy-to-use espresso machine picks that do most of the work for you, check out our guide to the Best Latte and Automatic Espresso Machines.

Also, be sure to check out our other coffee guides, like the Best Drip Coffee Makers, Best Cold Brew Makers, Best Aeropresses, Best Coffee Pod Machines, Best Coffee Subscriptions, and Best Coffee Grinders.

Updated November 2026: We’ve added information on Meraki’s second-run release and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

Sources indicate that san Francisco-based Fellow is almost certainly the most innovative and tech-forward coffee machine manufacturer of the moment. And rarely has an espresso machine so swiftly changed what I want from the best espresso makers as the Fellow Series 1, which started shipping in early 2026. Sure, the temperature control is admirable, with a patented heating technology that threads the needle between the fast heating of a thermoblock and the stability of a boiler. Automatic milk frothing is about as good and as fast as it gets. The dial and LED-screen controls are intuitive. And the device is compact, conserving both counter space and airspace.

Sources indicate that but the real game-changing addition with this machine is the way Fellow has introduced tight pressure control and shot profiles to the non-geek home espresso landscape. Almost every other espresso machine on the market just sorta aims at 9 bars of pressure and shrugs. The Series 1 offers profiles for light, medium, or dark roast that change pressure based on what's right for each bean—keeping dark roasts classic but pulling longer shots and dialing back pressure on light-roast beans. Other profiles, like turbo shots or “Modern Arc,” cater to the modern yen for espresso with less bitterness.

According to recent reports, after testing for weeks, I'm sold. You'd pay at least double to find this feature on any other espresso machine. And no device lets you play with pressure as easily as the Fellow, even before a planned firmware patch that'll allow you to sync profiles through Fellow's phone app. The app remains mostly a placeholder for now, offering tutorials and education but TBD functionality. But Fellow's track record building out the app on my top-pick drip coffee machine, the Fellow Aiden, gives me confidence this is a temporary blip. Volumetric controls still need tweaking, and the removable water reservoir can only be removed straight up from the device, requiring significant clearance.

But even with these early quirks, the Fellow Series 1 remains the most impressive espresso machine I've tested in the past couple of years. And it's changed what I want from espresso machines in the future. The Series 1 might already be the most-hyped machine of 2026. But this time, the hype is warranted.

The Barista Express had been our top pick for years, a Goldilocks choice in terms of price, versatility, and performance. It remains among the most popular espresso machines in the world (and possibly the most popular, period) for good reason. The Barista Express produces consistent pressure for espresso, its steam wand is excellent, and the built-in grinder makes it an all-in-one device. Its mostly metal construction, easy cleaning, and other thoughtful touches make it a faithful companion. My WIRED colleague Julian Chokkattu has been using his machine happily for seven years. And its price, which drops regularly during sales events, makes it accessible to mere mortals. For those who want a built-in grinder but don't want to spend four figures, this is an easy recommendation.

Competitors have taken direct aim at the Express with impressive semiautomatic entries like the Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier ($599) and Luxe Cafe Pro (see below), plus the De'Longhi La Specialista Opera ($900). Each of these offers more options, including cold espresso, with similar grind quality. For now, WIRED's years of testing and vetting the Barista Express, and Breville's good customer service reputation, keep the Express as my top recommendation. But in the meantime, I wouldn't be sad to see the Barista Express updated to better Baratza burrs on that built-in grinder, as Breville has done with its more expensive machines.

Sources indicate that upgrade pick: The Barista Express is a great mix of price and performance. But Breville's true top-line semiautomatic machine is the Breville Oracle Jet ($1,980 on Amazon), a touchscreen device with a better grinder that'll also offer better control and easier milk frothing and can guide you through everything from the proper bean grind to how to make a proper flat white, cappuccino, or espresso martini.

Recent findings suggest that A classic espresso machine rewards effort with nuance and beauty. And the Diletta Mio is everything a classic Italian-made espresso machine should be. It's compact, stylish, built to last, and brews circles around the competition. It's also a simple joy to use, wrote former WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey. It feels a bit analog, like an heirloom-quality stand mixer, but also sports sophisticated features like a PID (proportional-integral-derivative) temperature controller—a wee processor with an algorithm that keeps brew temperatures stable. Among traditional espresso machines that require a separate grinder, this is the one WIRED recommends.

Upgrade: WIRED's upgrade pick, the Diletta Bello ($1,899), is for advanced beanheads who love a sensitive machine. On the Bello, every difference makes a difference: every micron of grind size, or slight gradation of tamping pressure, will produce a different cup of espresso. But when you've dialed in your bean, the Bello is beautifully faithful—offering shot after shot of caramely crema and rich espresso.

The Bambino is little, fast, low-cost, and convenient—about as wide as a one-dollar bill. There are no apparent frills and no grinder: just a steam wand for silky milk and a choice between single or double shots. But look under the hood of this $300 beauty and you'll note features that are hallmarks of much more expensive machines: a thermoblock for immediate heating and a PID (proportional, integral, derivative) temperature controller that makes for consistent brew temps usually out of reach at this price range.

Which is to say it's a wee machine that pulls far above its weight class. Pair your Bambino with a good mid-level grinder and you'll be making beautiful cups with counter space to spare, for a total of $500.

Upgrade: The Breville Bambino Plus ($500) is hardier and slightly bigger and offers automatic milk frothing.

The Rancilio Silvia Pro is one of WIRED's longtime favorite dual-boiler espresso machines, packed with pro-level features and built to last seemingly forever, with few plastic parts. For far less than half the price, there's the Silvia M: the sleek, smaller-footprint, single-boiler cousin. What's the diff? There'll be a little bit more lag time between shots, if multiple people want espresso immediately. But you'll get that same high-quality metal build, and consistent water temp and steam pressure. This means well-extracted, café-grade espresso.

Note that the Silvia is notoriously sensitive, so it's not for beginners. It's also famously long-lasting, repairable, and able to be endlessly modified, and so it's birthed its own society of cult devotees. Just like buying a Land Cruiser or a Jeep, you'll end up with new friends. And if people online are to be believed, a lot of the OG Silvias have been chugging along for literal decades.

It has been revealed that it's tough to find a reliable espresso machine in the $200 range—and Italian coffee machine organization De'Longhi has long dominated the WIRED Gear team's favorite no-nonsense, low-budget espresso picks. The new De'Longhi Classic (previously branded as “Linea Classic”) is shiny chrome, with buttons for steam and your choice of single or double shots. It likewise sports a rare-at-this-price-point pressure gauge, a 15-bar pump, and an updated thermoblock system for fast heating.

The small touches matter. The steam wand has enough oomph to create some rudimentary latte art, if that’s your thing. And there's enough clearance between the portafilter and drip tray to fit a coffee or cappuccino mug, as opposed to a tiny espresso cup. But this said, after learning a few fun tricks from coffee influencer Lance Hedrick, I'm now also revisiting our previous extreme budget pick, De'Longhi Stilosa.

This guide is mostly dedicated to machines that make more classic espresso—the finicky kind that's harder to navigate and might leave coffee grounds on your counter. This sophisticated bean-to-cup De'Longhi Rivelia is a little different. It's my top pick among super-automatic machines that'll have you just fill a hopper with a half-bag of beans, then press a button. After helping you choose the right grinder settings, and asking how you like your coffee among well more than a dozen options, this touchscreen device will grind, and brew, and then froth up your milk for you.

Even the milk frother is about the easiest I've used, and it works with a single button-press once you've adjusted the foam density for drinks from dense flat white to frothy cappuccino. Heck, my mom was able to figure it out within a day, and so was my father. Even better, the Rivelia offers two swappable bean hoppers, an unheard-of luxury among similar devices that'll allow you to switch easily to decaf late in the day.

It has been revealed that note, however, that automatic machines like this Rivelia tend to make somewhat different coffee from what you'll get from other machines on this list. It grinds a bit coarser, leading to less unpredictability but also less intensity. If you're a milk lover, this likely won't matter much—and you may instead prize the simple ease with which you can have a frothing latte. Vodka lovers will find the same, when mixing cold espresso shots with the device.

It has been revealed that ever wonder why an espresso shot is sometimes called a pull? In the beginning, baristas used a lever to create the necessary pressure to extract espresso. And there's still a real satisfaction to literally pulling your own espresso, reviewer Jaina Grey noted. There’s no milk steamer, no boiler, no power cable. This thing is powered by a human, namely you.

Recent findings suggest that load it up with coffee and water per the manufacturer’s instructions and give it a good press. There’s also a pressure gauge to make sure you're hitting the target. Think of it like one of those strongman games at a carnival, except that the reward is delicious espresso.

How Do I Test Espresso Machines?

It has been revealed that over the past decade, WIRED has tested dozens of espresso makers to find our favorites. The process, in part, is simple. We brew a whole lot of coffee. I’ve written about coffee for more than a decade on both the East and West Coasts, including my hometown coffee mecca of Portland, Oregon. Other current and past WIRED espresso testers—who include former baristas and longtime coffee writers—include Jaina Grey, Jeffrey Van Camp, Kat Merck, Tyler Shane, Pete Cottell, and Scott Gilbertson.

Industry observers note that on each machine that’s capable, I make and assess at least four styles of drink, on multiple roasts and beans: a basic 2:1 espresso, an Americano, a latte, and a cappuccino. On machines that advertise a wacky array of drinks, I test each one. This includes any newfangled coldspresso and head-scratching variations on a “long.” It also includes, if science dictates, espresso martinis. And I test to see whether a machine can be dialed to both dark roasts and lighter roasts.

I might make many dozens of coffees to dial in a machine and truly understand it, and on any of my top picks I've made at least fifty drinks. Sometimes, alas, you understand a machine’s shortcomings far sooner—and so some of our less-recommended devices are dismissed a bit earlier.

What I’m looking for is nuance, aromatics, beauty, sensitivity to the characteristics of each bean, and the satisfying texture of fully integrated milk. But also, I’m looking for ease, the thoughtful touches that make an espresso maker something you can fall in love with.

Industry observers note that I test whether the hot water spout splatters, whether descaling requires a degree in hydrology, whether the brewing temperature is consistent, and whether the latte milk gets silked. I’m truly terrible at latte art, but whether it’s possible is a straightforward test of the body of the frothed milk. I test the airier foam of cappuccinos and compare manual and automatic milk frothing on machines that try to froth milk for you. I test how fast the wand steams and whether it’s easy to fully integrate milk before the dang thing starts to burn your milk.

It has been revealed that on machines with built-in grinders, I both assess the grind and weigh the dose—and then weigh it again. And then again. Consistency is the hobgoblin of little cups. I also test multiple grind settings to make sure the grind is consistent.

In a recent development, on any semiautomatic machine that decides the shot size for you, I test this to see whether you're getting a ristretto or a lungo by default. Then I resolve never to say the word “lungo” again.

I don’t generally take apart the machines I’m sent, but I do quite often look up videos of people who do—and look at how the thing’s constructed under the hood.

How I Select Espresso Machines to Review.

In part, we select machines to test by looking at the espresso makers with long track records of making good espresso machines—people with long tails in the industry and good track records of customer support. Names like Breville, De'Longhi, La Marzocco, and Rancilio. But also, I listen. I read. I ask every coffee-obsessive in my life. I pay attention to the newest releases, follow trade indicates, watch Youtube videos, and spend a lot of time tracking down not just the obious big names but the unexpected recommendations.

I often also look at how accessible each machine will be to most users. Espresso isn’t just a finicky process: It’s finicky by design. The most sensitive and sophisticated traditional machines are responsive to every tiny variation in the coffee grind and every fluctuation in the water temperature. The deepest bean geeks want this: They want the control, the frustration, the vision quest.

It has been revealed that but I also know that most of you out there aren’t looking to be in an abusive relationship with your coffee machine. Few want to wake up to feelings of inadequacy, brought on by a machine that costs as much as a used car. And so what I look for is the espresso machines that can pull lovely character from each bean, but also make this easy on you.

In a recent development, this means that our top picks, the ones I recommend to most people, tend to fall in the semiautomatic camp: They’re the ones that offer the best coffee with the least effort. Finding this balance is delicate and often rewarding. It used to be that a built-in grinder was a recipe for blown shots, sadness, or pressurized portafilters with less character. But year by year, espresso machine makers get better at this goal.

Industry observers note that the lowest-cost machines I recommend tend to offer more forgiving pressurized filter baskets as options, even though these sacrifice a bit of nuance for forgiveness, because I don’t want to assume you’re pairing a $200 espresso machine with a $2,000 coffee grinder. Although I know some of you do this, especially with our beloved Breville Bambino.

In a recent development, but hey, if you’re a tinkerer for life, and want to join modding groups? We recommend a machine for you, too. Mostly so you can disagree on Reddit, and explain why your favorite is better.

What Beans Are Best for Espresso?

In a recent development, first off, there's no such thing as “espresso beans,” whatever it states on the bag you buy. Espresso beans are coffee beans, ground finely enough to be pressed into service as espresso.

Recent findings suggest that but traditionally, espresso is made with darker-roast beans that best elicit the deep, chocolatey notes of classic Italian espresso. In fact, most machines you use are probably designed with dark-roast beans in mind: Darker beans grind easier, extract easier, and are a bit more homogeneous across the market. And so when someone writes “espresso roast” or “espresso blend” on their grind, that's often what they mean.

According to recent reports, does that mean dark roast is the only espresso? Of course not. Modern craft and premium coffee roasters in the United States have begun trending toward medium and medium-dark roasts that offer a bit more balance, character, and even a little acidity—beans that have more aromatics, and more individuality. Some, including me, love experimenting with truly light roasts, including the lightest of natural-processed beans that let me brew up espresso that tastes like strawberries.

It's up to you. But note that the lighter the roast, the more you'll need to adjust grind and temperature to accommodate—and sometimes even go off-script entirely. (See here for an explainer on light-roast espresso.) But the classic recommendations for espresso? Pulling a 25- to 30-second shot, at a steady 9 bars of pressure, at a 2:1 ratio for a standard shot? These were all designed for traditional dark-roast beans.

Industry observers note that one thing that's true, however, is that you should use fresh beans. They'll taste better and more aromatic, sure. But stale beans exposed to oxygen also make it technically difficult to make good espresso: they've begun to break down, often allow channeling, and are more likely to lead to a less evenly extracted shot with funny off-flavors.

Obviously, fresh beans are easiest to obtain from a local roaster, and on the plus side you'll be able to ask the baristas there how best to make espresso from their beans. But when in doubt in a supermarket, look for a roast date on the bag. If you can't find it, or if your beans were roasted in Italy and sent on a ship? Chances are they're not fresh. And your espresso will be worse. For fresh beans delivered to your house, check out WIRED's guide to the best coffee subscriptions.

Espresso Accessories That Make for Great Cups.

If you're spending this much on an espresso machine, you'll want to invest in a good grinder and even a scale, as well as a few other devices that make your shots better, and your life a little easier.

An espresso-capable grinder: If your espresso machine doesn't come with a grinder, you'll need one. Preground bag beans are especially difficult to use when making espresso, and will likely lead to off-flavors or channeling. But not just any grinder will do. You'll need a good grinder that can grind consistent beans finely enough for espresso. WIRED's top-pick Baratza Encore ESP is always a good choice—positioned squarely at the fulcrum where more expensive grinders begin to offer diminishing returns.

It has been revealed that an accurate scale with a timer: Most grinders, and a goodly portion of espresso machines, do not offer a precise scale. But a precise scale is what you need to get espresso ratios right. WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu loved the Acaia brew-by-weight scale ($400) that automatically connects to the La Marzocco Linea Mini and a few other devices via its companion app. But a far less sophisticated scale can still help you measure your shot size and control the dose you want on each espresso shot. If you're not precious about beauty, there's always this low-cost, little no-name scale. It's accurate to a 10th of a gram, and has a timer to boot.

In a recent development, the best knockbox: When you're done with that portafilter filled with coffee grounds, what do you do with it? Beat it against the side of a trashcan? Dig out those grounds into the sink? Nah. You need a good knock box. And somehow this jobby-job from Breville is the best one I've ever found. It's sturdy, the cross bar is in the right spot so that the grinds dump cleanly into the bin, and the bottom has enough grip that the box doesn't scoot around on the counter. Simplicity is competence.

Not all steaming pitchers are created equal, notes WIRED contributing reviewer (and former barista) Pete Cottell. As opposed to the sad piece of aluminum that probably came with your espresso maker, this Brewista offers thick walls for heat retention, a precision tip for expert latte pours, and a thermometer sticker on its side so you can get a rough gauge of milk temperature without hunting down an actual thermometer. It can also take a beating. This is your new frothing pitcher.

Recent findings suggest that breville Oracle Jet for $2,000: The Breville Oracle Jet is my previous top pick for threading that delicate needle between ease and deliciousness, before getting displaced by my new top-pick Fellow device. The Oracle Jet remains a powerful and frankly beautiful stainless-steel machine, with sterling temperature control and a solid built-in grinder that uses the same conical burrs as the excellent Baratza Encore ESP ($200). This Oracle Jet will pull beautiful nuances from beans ranging from berry-light to chocolate dark, on drinks ranging from an Americano to a flat white to “cold espresso” best placed in a martini. And yet the Jet's easily accessible for anyone who can figure out an iPhone, with a touchscreen tutorial, digital guidance on finding the right grind for each bean, and automatic tamping and steaming. You'll be nose-deep in a cappuccino within 20 minutes of pulling this thing out of the box. Note that manual milk steaming with the Jet's powerful wand is still better than the automatic version.

Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro for $750: Tradition is the opposite of what Ninja does. This is the manufacturer that made the soft-serve Swirl, the Slushi, and the portable air fryer. Ninja is all about the extras. And Ninja doesn't judge. And so of course Ninja jumped in with both feet on cold-foam coldspresso. In fact, the fresh Luxe Cafe Pro makes the best cold foam out of any espresso machine I've tried, with a whisk that whips up plant milk or cow milk into thick, creamy, dense, beautiful froth—ready for your ridiculously complicated cold caramel-vanilla latte TikTok recipe. What I didn't expect was that Ninja would also nail the fundamentals so well, on only its second entry into the espresso market. The relatively accurate by-weight dosing is nice. So is the excellent steam wand that also outpaces most contenders on automatic hot foaming, adjustable to multiple densities of foam. The Pro clears up some oversights in the previous-model Premier, including an easy tamping lever, and a hot water spout. Maintenance, whether descaling or purging, is also as easy as it gets. Just don't use this grinder with light roast beans. Medium or dark only.

Breville Oracle Dual Boiler for $3,000: This update to the previous Breville Dual Boiler espresso machine is a powerful, truly impressive machine in many regards. It combines the easy touchscreen operation and automatic dosing and tamping of WIRED's previous top-pick Oracle Jet with a welcome “manual” mode that lets you play with pre-infusion and bloom while monitoring a digital pressure gauge on the touchscreen. I kinda love this as an exercise in future-retro design—or whatever the inverse of steampunk is—but also as a means of really controlling my shot, and getting a lot more crema and body out of it. The dual boiler heats up very fast—like four minutes fast—and gives you the wonderful temperature stability and consistency you expect from a dual boiler, plus the ability to steam milk and make espresso simultaneously. The production model I received had a very tight portafilter fit, which loosened up after the first 30 shots or so but initially required some muscle. I also haven't been able to get good results with lighter-roast beans, which led to the occasional under-filled portafilter that had to be retamped manually. We'll update as we resolve those quirks, but can attest that for medium to dark beans, this Dual Boiler is an absolute beast.

In a recent development, meraki Espresso Machine for $1,999: When former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage first tested this high-design “steampunk gasworks” of an espresso machine, he loved the features for the price, including a Timemore grinder that grinds by weight, PID temperature control, easy pre-infusion, and another scale under the brewer that lets you control output. He did not, however, love having to overrotate the portafilter for a proper fit, or the wackily complicated descaling procedure. I’ve since tested the second run of this machine (the one you’ll be getting if you buy right now) and did not have any trouble with the portafilter. You’ll also get 45 grind settings instead of the original 30, though we were hard-pressed to discern a real difference from the additional 15. —Kat Merck.

Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier for $600: Ninja has already released an upgraded Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro version ($750) after its espresso machine debut. But its first device, the Luxe Cafe Premier, is already a corker, a low-priced all-in-one with cold brew, coffee, espresso, excellent milk frothing, and unexpected luxury features like a built-in scale so the grinder can dose by weight. The device can feel either overstuffed or generous, depending on who you are. Either way, this damn near unseated the Breville Barista Express as WIRED’s mid-tier top pick, aside from a few leaks and sensible caution about its durability.

It has been revealed that de'Longhi La Specialista Opera for $800: Speaking of espresso makers that came running at Breville, this Opera is a beautifully forgiving semiautomatic machine that makes excellent espresso in the medium- to dark-roast range, with non-pressurized portafilter baskets that make for a nice and surprisingly subtle cup. It’s the best De'Longhi espresso machine I’ve tested, in many ways, among the semiautomatic camp. The Opera sports a lot of options—including dose and temperature control—while remaining refreshingly analog with its satisfying metal frame, metal buttons, and prominent pressure gauge. Cold brew is a perk for those who like milk. The grinder is decent, though its 15 settings might not offer enough sensitivity to pull the best from each roast. One could wish for a removable hopper and a sturdier tamping lever. But if you or your partner love cold coffee drinks or espresso martinis, this gives comparable Brevilles a strong run for the money.

De'Longhi La Specialista Touch for $800: De'Longhi’s new Touch, released this year, isn't merely a touchscreen version of the very analog Opera—though it is just as handsome as the Opera. Instead, it offers a very specific set of trade-offs. Like De'Longhi's Rivelia, there's a bean-assist function that you can save for each bean you like. It also has a better steam wand, with the ability to read the temperature of the milk you're steaming as you steam it. In fact, it's maybe more intuitive overall. But it doesn't quite offer the easy customization on temperature, shot time, or ratios. The cold brew is not quite as well-dialed as the Opera. The Touch is an Italian machine on training wheels, designed for Italian-style medium to dark shots. This should work for most people, but minus a pressure bar or a shot timer, it can also feel like a bit of a black box.

La Marzocco Linea Mini for $6,600: WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu spent two weeks with La Marzocco's Linea Mini, a home version of the fancy espresso machines you'll see in coffee shops around the world. The price may be eye-searing, but Chokkattu did find the resulting elixir to be absolutely fantastic—and the same went for La Marzocco's customer service while Chokkattu was dialing in his machine. It offers a lot of room for experimentation, and it sports a killer cool-touch steam wand that froths milk in seconds.

De'Longhi Stilosa for $150: The Stilosa was our top budget pick for years. It's still a good budget pick, and it often goes on sale for less than $100. You're not going to get high-end features like a pressure gauge or built-in grinder, and it's a little plasticky. But what the Stilosa does provide is everything you need to make great espresso at home: a solid portafilter, a reliable steam pump, and a steaming wand. It is a little light, so you'll want to brace it when you mount and dismount the portafilter (or it might slide around on you). After brewing cup after cup of espresso, the Stilosa never indicated signs of slowing or breaking down the way many inexpensive machines can. In fact, we're now revisiting the Stilosa as our budget pick, after catching a few tips on how to use the Stilosa for light roast espresso.

It has been revealed that breville Barista Express Impress for $800: This espresso machine is the more tricked-out sibling of the Breville Barista Express. It includes more grind and dosing settings and automates some of the more complicated parts of brewing consistently good espresso, like getting just the right amount of beans ground per shot.

Breville Dual Boiler for $1,600: The previous-generation Breville Dual Boiler is an absolute tank of an espresso machine. It's huge. It's heavy. It makes amazing espresso. But while its size makes brewing espresso feel luxurious, it does eat up a lot of space and needs a little time to heat up, versus newer Brevilles like the Oracle Jet that favor thermoblock-style heaters. But a dual boiler does mean you can brew shot after shot, with steamed milk and hot water at the same time, without having to wait in between shots. The new Breville Oracle Dual Boiler ($3,000) is already on the market, but you can still pick up the previous generation for half the price.

In a recent development, cuisinart EM-160 Slim for $250: The lowest-cost espresso maker from Cuisinart's upcoming espresso line is among the slimmer espresso machines out there, less than 7 inches across. This makes it a treasure for certain kitchens. The espresso quality is about what you'd expect from a pressurized portafilter: smoother, less nuanced, but also pretty forgiving for beginners trying to dial in a bean. This'll be best for those who mix milk with their espresso. Same goes for the fast-dripped “cold espresso” option, which takes a couple minutes to complete and comes out a bit tannic, but mixes well with cold milk or a lot of ice. You'll need a grinder if you don't want sad supermarket beans.

According to recent reports, superkop Manual Espresso Maker for $800: This manual espresso machine is technically not a Jackie Chan movie. The Superkop is instead a quite finely engineered espresso device. It looks pretty, and unlike other manual espresso machines, you don't need a strong arm to use it. So if you want to pull espresso, but not pull it hard, the Superkop is your huckleberry. That stated, $600 is a lot of money for a manual device. Buy it if you know you'll love it.

Gevi Espresso Machine With Grinder and Milk Frother for $350: WIRED contributing reviewer Pete Cottell prized the pressure control and built-in grinder on this Gevi espresso machine, when you take into account the near-unfathomable low price for a machine with this functionality. Alas, a somewhat erratic steam wand makes it hard to recommend.

Recent findings suggest that cuisinart EM-640 Espresso Bar for $650: Cuisinart rolled in with some ambition on this semiautomatic espresso machine, with a built-in grinder and a non-pressurized, bottomless portafilter meant to play in the same sandbox as Breville's top devices. Alas, I really couldn't get consistency on either dosing or grinding from the device's built-in grinder—and the system for customizing the dose in particular was mostly wild guesswork. This all added up to botched shots, wild spray from the portafilter, and none of the ease one wants from a semiautomatic.

De'Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo for $700: This semiautomatic De'Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo comes with a built-in burr grinder and makes great espresso right out of the box, and is slimmer than other espresso machines in its category. It does have quirks: It includes a little plastic adapter needed to attach the portafilter to the grinder spout, and a little stepstool for your espresso cup to keep the coffee from splashing. It’s a good machine, but I'd upgrade to the Opera any day of the week.

Industry observers note that 9to5Mac is sponsored by Sony: Score Sony’s INZONE noise-canceling earbuds for 38% off. These deliver immersive 360 Spatial Sound, active noise canceling, low-latency wireless connectivity, and much more.

With iPhone Handoff, you can use the same phone number on two different iPhones. Your number automatically moves between the two phones, depending on which one you pick up. This includes calls, voicemail, messages, and Find My location.

It has been revealed that simply unlock whichever device you want to use and you’re ready to go. Other data synced with iCloud will automatically update across your devices. Third-party apps work across both devices, following each app’s own syncing behavior.

iPhone Handoff is available on iOS 27 and later. The phones must be connected to Wi-Fi, share the same Apple Account, use Messages in iCloud, and be signed into FaceTime and iMessage with the same Apple Account.

Sources indicate that the biggest limiting factor of iPhone Handoff is that it requires carrier support. At the moment, just three carriers support the feature:.

In a statement in September, the carrier noted that its focus “remains on delivering innovations that make life simpler and keep customers connected with confidence.” The carrier noted that there “could be potential in capabilities like iPhone Handoff,” but that customers should use “existing eSIM activation and transfer options” instead.

No other carriers have promised support for iPhone Handoff, so it’s unclear how swiftly the feature will expand around the world.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia shares fell around 7% on Tuesday, paring a massive Monday rally that was sparked by the return of Jensen Huang as CEO.

Industry observers note that other U.S. semiconductor stocks also opened lower after posting strong gains Monday. Micron declined 10%, Marvell Technology lost 8%, Arm Holdings dropped 8% and AMD shed 10% in morning trading.

It has been revealed that huang, who resigned as CEO of Nvidia earlier this month after admitting to an extramarital affair, was reinstated on Monday. The stock closed over 30% higher following the news of Huang's return.

The organization's board of directors stated it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him.

President Donald Trump also claimed he was personally involved in Huang's return. The president told CNBC that he spoke with the chipmaker's board before it reversed course and reinstated its co-founder.

"I made the deal," Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers on Monday during an interview on "Squawk on the Street.".

Trump noted Nvidia's board asked for guarantees that Huang, who resigned less than two weeks ago, was not a threat to national security.

"And we gave them assurances, at least with everything we know," the president said. "We believe he's fine. He's absolutely fine.".

After Huang's reinstatement, several Wall Street analysts turned more bullish on the stock and upgraded their ratings on Nvidia.

"We believe reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang RETURNS Investor CONFIDENCE in the AI trade," Mizuho analysts wrote in a note on Monday.

Huang and Nvidia have been central to the AI story, supplying the chips that power AI and financing companies across the ecosystem.

The tech giant remains under scrutiny as questions remain about Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy.

The U.S. is investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed, the company where she worked. Questions also remain regarding whether Nvidia chips are making their way into China despite export controls.

Sources indicate that huang is set to publicly testify in front of the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who is set to take over the Committee in January, called Huang's reinstatement "reckless.".

Industry observers note that "The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Warren noted in a statement on Monday.

Huang is also expected to sit for a closed-door interview with the House Foreign Affairs, Intelligence and China Select committees on Dec. 1.

"Reinstatement should not be confused with the end of scrutiny," Bank of America said in a note on Monday. "We therefore expect elevated attention around governance, China/export controls, customer relationships and compliance to persist even with the CEO question resolved.".

— CNBC's Luke Fountain, Seema Mody and Dan Mangan contributed to this report.

#2511. One terminal command gave my forgotten Android device a desk job

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1207 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

One terminal command gave my forgotten Android device a desk job

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1207 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones.
  • Recent findings suggest that I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate.
  • Industry observers note that getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn’t have been simpler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My kitchen junk drawer used to hold takeout menus and coupons, but it has since become a storage spot for old tablets or phones. Like me, you probably have a few devices lying around that are perfectly functional but don’t meet your daily driving needs. It’s tucked out of view, living out its life in a drawer until being erased and donated after someone asks why you’re holding onto outdated, unused devices. Thankfully, PhoneBox has a solution. You weren’t hoarding old tech; you were waiting for the proper use.

Recent findings suggest that I had an old AllDoCube iPlay 50 mini Pro 8.4-inch tablet that seemed like the perfect candidate. I bought the tablet second-hand as a possible major-screen gaming and emulation tablet to use with a telescopic control deck, but I swiftly found I vastly preferred just using a dedicated device. Since that realization, this decent little unit has lived its life in “the drawer.”.

Industry observers note that getting PhoneBox up and running on my tablet and PC couldn’t have been simpler. After making sure that the Android tablet was in developer mode, the process was as easy as plugging the tablet in to my PC via USB and executing a single copied command in my Linux terminal. The script downloaded the PhoneBox 0.9.29 software for my PC, verified the downloaded checksum against the release, and walked me through a few quick Y/N installation questions. The script offers to create a systemd user service, so the desktop agent launches after initial login, and even asks if you’d like it to install the PhoneBox APK to your connected Android device.

It has been revealed that I already had developer mode initialized on the tablet but had to go back and allow ADB over USB in settings. The total installation time from copying the script from the project website to everything running on my PC and tablet was less than a minute. The app is MIT-licensed, works on Android 5.0 or later, and requires sideloading, since it is not available on the Google Play Store.

Credit: Nick Indge Credit: Nick Indge.

In a recent development, the installation script also prints its own uninstall script before it finishes. So often these days, getting rid of an unwanted app feels more difficult than installing it, so I appreciate the straightforward approach the developer has implemented.

The first time you fire up PhoneBox, you get live performance and diagnostic information from your PC, along with several pages of optional content that can be tweaked for your local setup to display information that’s pertinent to your uses.

Where PhoneBox really starts to shine is the widget catalog—a collection of free add-ons that can be added as pages to the tablet’s cycling page layouts. There are more general widgets, such as RSS feeds that display news highlights from your chosen sources, or simple displays like timers or world clocks.

It has been revealed that I opted for a few different widgets that caught my eye. One let me view my library of installed Steam titles and launch them on my PC with a simple tap of the tablet screen. Another allows me to control smart home entities hosted by my Home Assistant server. I was controlling the lights in my office from my tablet within seconds of adding the widget. It’s brilliant.

Setting up additional widgets is as simple as adding them to the page layout from the PC’s web interface and hitting save. As soon as I updated things from the PC, the connected tablet immediately began reflecting the changes. I haven’t had the chance to test most of the 131 current options in the widget catalog, but the ones I did try were simple to modify and worked on the first try.

While I didn’t have any major issues with PhoneBox, I did notice a couple of early annoyances along the way. Windows users should be aware that the PC companion app on that OS is at the moment unsigned, and they should expect a SmartScreen notification when attempting to install the software.

All control settings live in the web interface rather than the phone or tablet you’re connecting. When I first started messing with PhoneBox, I noticed it displayed my weather location as Tallinn. Nothing against the capital of Estonia, but that’s not weather information that does me much good here in the US Midwest. When I went into the widget settings to change the report location, there was nothing to be found. It turns out that you have to change those settings from the general user preferences section rather than within the widget itself. Not a deal-breaker by any means, but a slight hiccup for someone who was upcoming to the software.

Connecting the Android tablet with my PC over USB was totally painless, but I never got the wireless route to work in my testing. Consumers are meant to generate a QR code from the PhoneBox web interface on their PC and connect it to their device by scanning the code with their phone/tablet. Every time I tried to scan the code from my device’s camera app, the tablet refused. There’s no QR scanner built into the PhoneBox app, so if your camera app won’t cooperate, the documented path dead-ends. USB was my intended route anyway and works great, but if you’re planning a wireless-only setup, be prepared for possible friction. The documented flow needs your device camera to open the pairing link, and mine wasn’t in the mood.

It has been revealed that these minor gripes should be smoothed over before the release of 1.0. The project is early, but it seems to be moving quickly. I tested and installed PhoneBox version 0.9.29, which was one of several releases pushed to the project’s GitHub in as many days. One item of history worth noting: On November 20, the project published a high-severity security advisory covering versions 0.9.23 and earlier. The vulnerability potentially allowed another app running on the connected Android device to execute commands or receive stored credentials from the host PC. The flaw no longer existed by the time I tested the package in version 0.9.29, but it’s a good reminder that you’re installing something with deep system access and should exercise appropriate caution.

As long as you’re part of the group that has an old phone or tablet lying around somewhere, and these days I expect that most of us are, then it’s an emphatic yes. Repurposing old devices to find newly introduced lives is one of the things that keeps me a tech hobbyist. I love finding genuinely useful and practical applications for devices that have been pushed aside by their manufacturers in favor of the latest and greatest in the lineup.

PhoneBox took a tablet that was forgotten in a junk drawer and destined for donation and gave it a upcoming lease on life. I haven’t spent a single penny, but I now have a useful secondary display on my desk. The tablet is powered via a dedicated USB port on my PC, and only goes to sleep when my main monitor displays do. Go dig through those mystery drawers in your house, because this one is worthwhile.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Samsung might be gearing up for another significant change to its flagship phone cameras.
  • Industry observers note that the claim comes from well-known leaker Ice Universe, who shared the alleged changes on X.
  • For the uninitiated, the laser autofocus module is supposed to emit an infrared beam and calculate the time it takes to bounce back from a subject, then use the distance information to assist the camera in locking focus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Samsung might be gearing up for another significant change to its flagship phone cameras. A latest leak suggests Samsung is likely to ditch the laser autofocus hardware, possibly taking the 3x telephoto camera with it. That’s two changes to the rear camera system, and while neither is necessarily a recipe for photographic trouble, it does bring up an interesting question: what does Samsung intend to use instead?

Industry observers note that the claim comes from well-known leaker Ice Universe, who shared the alleged changes on X. Samsung has been using laser autofocus in its Ultra phones since the Galaxy S21 Ultra, so this is a departure from a camera setup the company has used for several generations.

For the uninitiated, the laser autofocus module is supposed to emit an infrared beam and calculate the time it takes to bounce back from a subject, then use the distance information to assist the camera in locking focus.

Sources indicate that this is particularly helpful in low-light situations, where traditional phase-detection autofocus (PDAF) can struggle. But laser autofocus has its own limitations. It struggles with distant subjects, bright sunlight and moving objects.

Industry observers note that that doesn't necessarily mean the S27 Ultra will have a worse camera. Autofocus technology has come a long way. Both dual-pixel and all-pixel autofocus can calculate the distance to a subject by using multiple light-sensitive areas across the image sensor. This technology is already being used in some of Samsung’s other flagship devices, so the ditching of a separate laser module is not necessarily a step backward.

It’s also rumored that Samsung might utilize its fresh 200MP ISOCELL HP6 sensor for the Galaxy S27 Ultra and S27 Pro. Previous reports have indicated support for LOFIC, a technology that’s designed to improve HDR photography and preserve detail in the brightest and darkest parts of a photo. It’s not known if the new sensor will also introduce an advanced autofocus system as well.

Sources indicate that the bigger question is what these hardware changes portend for everyday photography. The lack of a dedicated 3x camera may mean more reliance on cropping the sensor for zoom ranges in between. The removal of laser autofocus may mean more reliance on the main sensor’s focusing system.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

None of these changes have been confirmed by Samsung, and we won’t see the Galaxy S27 family until the first quarter of 2027. Whether these rumored changes are a smart play for newer imaging tech or just another instance of stripping out useful hardware to cut costs is something buyers will want answered before splashing out flagship money.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the debate over the wisdom and safety of using Meta’s Muse AI agent continues as the app rolls out in the UK. It follows a warning by a number of regulatory bodies about the potential risks of AI agents ….

Meta yesterday confirmed the UK availability of Muse.

It has been revealed that muse, Meta’s personal Al agent, is now available to adults in the UK. Think of it as a helping hand for the jobs that pile up, like chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or keeping on top of the school calendar. To get those jobs done you can connect Muse to the apps you already use, from your email and calendar to the retailer apps you shop on.

A forum representing four different UK regulatory bodies last month issued a warning about the potential dangers involved in using AI agents. The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum noted:.

AI agents may amplify and accelerate risks and introduce new ones. These risks may increase as the capabilities of personal agents grow and adoption rises. Questions of consumer protection, competition and data protection – for example the risk of fraud and scams, personal information sharing not in line with user expectations and misleading recommendations, decisions or information provided – must be addressed to ensure innovation develops in ways that earn and maintain public trust.

Meta has pushed back against suggestions that Muse has accessed personal data without permission, insisting that people are in control and must approve important actions. The organization has admitted to some “isolated incidents,” but states other reported breaches were either hallucinations or took place on internal versions of the app while undergoing testing. In a fresh blog post, Meta says:.

Muse only works with the apps and services you choose to connect it to, and you control the access it gets […] Once you’ve decided what Muse is connected to and what you want it to do, with your oversight, it can handle tasks like searching, comparing and planning for you. But before it does anything like sending an email or buying something, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your go-ahead. A separate security agent checks Muse’s actions and the information it sends out against the permissions you’ve granted. You can also choose how often it checks in with you in Settings.

Recent findings suggest that at the time of writing, Muse remains the second most popular free app in Apple’s US App Store, with more than 10 million downloads. We reported yesterday that some banks are already blocking AI agents, while others are warning that they will not be responsible for the consequences of any actions taken by them.

Frontier AI models that have yet to be released by OpenAI and Anthropic are reportedly reaching the point where employees believe they cannot be safely released or controlled, employees reportedly say.

Axios cites “more than two dozen” employees inside of OpenAI and Anthropic who are sounding warnings around unreleased models from both companies.

Sources indicate that while both OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude public models are increasingly powerful, these employees say that newly introduced models behind the scenes are starting to beat out the technical solutions for controlling them. This has led to debates between those who think they’ll be able to fix these problems, and others who believe companies should stop training new models altogether due to the risks.

If we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they’re actually smarter than us … they will in fact be able to trick us successfully. And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we’ve had at work up until now sort of go out the window.

The report goes out to point out that some researchers feel that executives at major AI companies have become “out of touch” with the severity of safety risks, though Axios was told that OpenAI is adopting latest safety practices while Anthropic said that “Keeping a model internal doesn’t make it safe,” adding that “we may slow down or hold back even when it costs us.”.

Thanksgiving Travel Will Be a Stormy Mess

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (868 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, expect travel headaches from coast to coast this week.
  • Industry observers note that A very active pattern draped across North America will keep the storm train running in the days ahead.
  • The stormy setup arrives at the peak travel time of the year in the US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, expect travel headaches from coast to coast this week. Several rounds of disruptive weather sweep are likely to cause delays at airports and make for challenging driving conditions just in time for the Thanksgiving long weekend.

Industry observers note that A very active pattern draped across North America will keep the storm train running in the days ahead. Potent systems rolling into the West Coast will bring disruptions from Seattle to San Francisco, where high tides could swamp airport runways. East of the Rockies, a major coastal storm expected to develop on Wednesday will generate widespread heavy rain and winds so gusty there’s a “significant chance” the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade could be balloonless for the first time in 55 years. The same system will also deliver the season’s first measurable snow in some areas.

The stormy setup arrives at the peak travel time of the year in the US. The Transportation Security Administration screened 3.1 million passengers to close out the long weekend in 2025, marking the agency’s highest passenger volume on record. And with the extreme weather this week is set to sweep across some of the country’s biggest travel hubs, it could upend the best-laid travel plans.

A persistent series of low-pressure systems will drag waves of heavy precipitation into the Pacific Northwest throughout the week, making delays and the occasional cancellation likely for flyers in Seattle and Portland.

The real risk for delays begins to pile up when rain and gusty winds follow a cold front into northern California on Tuesday night Though the worst of the rain will likely clear out in time for the bulk of Wednesday’s travel, flooding is still a major concern for low-lying highways and parts of San Francisco International Airport.

Sources indicate that forecasters expect a near-record king tide—that is, one of the highest tides of the year—on Tuesday and Wednesday. King tides are a normal occurrence, but this year’s will be exacerbated by record-high sea levels driven by the Super El Niño. The climate phenomenon has pushed warm water toward the coast, which takes up more space than cold water.

Monday’s forecast from the National Weather Service called for a high tide of 8.5 feet at the San Francisco gauge on Wednesday morning, which is just shy of the all-time record of 8.66 feet set in January 1983, another Super El Niño year.

Farther east, the atmospheric ingredients are lining up for a sprawling nor’easter to develop over the Southeast by Wednesday and move north through New England by the end of the week.

Recent findings suggest that widespread heavy rainfall will accompany the storm northward, potentially worsening highway traffic as commuters and vacationers alike navigate slick roads in gloomy conditions. Gusty winds will reduce visibility during heavy rainfall. Forecasters expect several inches of rain along the East Coast, especially along the Interstate 95 corridor between South Carolina and New York.

Industry observers note that airline delays are almost certain given the dreaded mix of precipitation, low clouds, and stiff winds. The greatest impacts are likely in Charlotte and Raleigh in North Carolina on Wednesday, followed by Washington, DC, Philadelphia, New York, and Boston on Thursday.

All these cities are home to major hubs for various airlines. Foul conditions at one of those airports can have ripple effects that lead to delayed or canceled flights down the line, including in cities where the weather is just fine. This may be the most impactful Thanksgiving weather since a nor’easter rolled up the East Coast on the Wednesday and Thursday of the holiday weekend in 2014. That storm hit the major hubs with high winds and heavy rain, as well as up to a foot of wet snow across much of the interior Northeast. The event led to thousands of cancelled and delayed flights. (The US also got a taste of travel trouble earlier this month when a Federal Aviation Administration ground stop left travelers stranded.).

The conditions could get so dire, that the Macy’s parade could go on but sans balloons. The parade will ground its balloons if there are sustained winds of 24 mph or gusts of 35 mph. The National Weather Service issued a high wind watch for New York City beginning Thursday morning, with winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts up to 60 mph possible, though when the nor’easter reaches New York will determine if the winds cross that crucial threshold during the parade.

It has been revealed that cold air wrapping into the western side of the same storm system could lead to the first measurable snow of the season throughout portions of the Midwest. Computer models are still a bit wishy-washy on exactly where and how much snow will fall, as the rain-snow line will depend on the precise track of the storm. As of Monday, the general consensus for a few inches of wet snow appears to focus on the St. Louis metro area east into central Illinois.

There’s some good news for travelers in the eastern US, at least: The nor’easter is expected to clear out by Saturday morning, which should hopefully reduce any snarls for travelers headed home on Sunday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Once again, Honor wants to burnish its Hollywood bona fides.

If there's one thing to expect from the launch of a newly introduced Honor phone, it's an attempt to burnish its Hollywood bona fides. The advent of the new Magic 9 Pro Max is a chance for the Chinese giant to, as usual, tell the world about how it's once again redefined mobile cinematography. It's the first proper Honor flagship — and second only to the Robot Phone — to benefit from its partnership with Arri. If you're unfamiliar, the German giant makes the Alexa cinema camera, which has shot at least six films which went on to win an Academy Award for cinematography. If nothing else, if your Instagram reel doesn't at least garner a nomination, you know it's not the hardware's fault.

It has been revealed that the Magic 9 Pro Max is the first Honor flagship to use the company's new industrial design first seen on its lower-end N series models. That includes a new camera plateau, albeit with a new color contrast back panel around the frame which puts me in mind of... something. Similarly, this is the first Honor flagship to get the Pro Max moniker, a suffix I don't think I've seen elsewhere in the rest of the mobile industry, but which sounds so cool that you think it might inspire copycats.

Sources indicate that nestled inside, you'll find a Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 system-on-chip with either 12GB or 16GB RAM and the choice of 256GB, 512GB or 1TB storage. Up front, it's packing a 6.8-inch, 2,868 x 1,320 LTPO OLED display with a 1-120Hz refresh rate and 10,000 nits peak brightness. That's paired with an 8,000mAh battery which can support up to 100W wired or 80W wireless charging. Rounding out the useful specs are Wi-Fi 7, space for two SIM cards as well as an eSIM and a 55-megapixel front-facing camera.

Industry observers note that of course, these are all just supporting players for the main event, the Arriflex-inspired triple camera system 'round back. It's equipped with a 200-megapixel, f/1.57 OIS primary lens and a 200-megapixel f/2.6 OIS telephoto, as well as a 50-megapixel f/2.0 ultra-wide camera. Of note is that Honor claims the primary lens has "gimbal" levels of optical stabilization to keep your shots as smooth as possible, no matter how you old it.

It has been revealed that to make use of all those megapixels, Honor is launching its first dedicated imaging processor, the H1, and grabbed plenty of Arri's know-how. Honor says the Magic 9 Pro Max uses an end-to-end cinematic workflow, shooting high-end video in Arri LogC3 — the tech giant's version of Log — as well as a series of Arri-created filters and color profiles you can apply to your footage. You'll have a pick of up to 87 Arri looks to apply to your footage, and you can even shoot in Cinema ratios like 2.39:1.

It has been revealed that to further bolster its credentials in this arena, Honor is launching a series of accessories in partnership with SmallRig. Equip your phone with the SmallRig camera cage and you'll be able to attach it to either the Honor-branded Teleconverter G200 or the Teleconverter G500. They'll increase the phone's focal length by either 200mm or 500mm, enabling you to shoot distances you'd struggle to capture with AI-enhanced imaging.

Honor's Magic 9 Pro Max is debuting in Malaysia, priced at RM 5,999 (approx $1,455) for the 12GB RAM / 512GB storage option. It'll arrive in the Middle East next month, and take its first bow in the West at some point in January.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The partnership is pulling human safety drivers from its Lucid Gravity SUVs ahead of an early 2027 commercial debut.﻿.

The partnership is pulling human safety drivers from its Lucid Gravity SUVs ahead of an early 2027 commercial debut.﻿.

According to recent reports, uber’s high-stakes robotaxi bet is officially ditching its human safety net. Nuro, Lucid, and Uber are starting fully driverless public road testing in the San Francisco Bay Area, with employee-only rides launching shortly after.

First unveiled in July 2025, this three-way alliance represents Uber’s aggressive comeback in autonomous ride-hailing, after having abandoned its own troubled in-house efforts years ago. By pulling human safety operators from behind the wheel of Lucid Gravity SUVs, the companies say they are clearing a critical hurdle toward a public launch. That debut is now slated for early 2027, marking a slight slip from the partnership’s original late-2026 target. When it finally goes live, it will pit Uber directly against entrenched rivals like Waymo and Zoox on their home turf.

Driverless testing kicks off across four South Bay cities—Palo Alto, Mountain View, Los Altos, and Sunnyvale—before expanding across the broader Bay Area next year. To fuel this push, Lucid has delivered more than 100 upgraded Gravity SUVs, up from the 75 engineering vehicles on the road earlier this year.

In a recent development, the automaker began building pre-production models in October to clear regulatory safety approvals, and it intends to start manufacturing the actual commercial fleet in the coming weeks. Each SUV is powered by Nuro’s Level 4 “Nuro Driver” system, pairing cameras, solid-state lidar, and radar with a roof-mounted LED “halo” that flashes a rider’s initials and pickup status.

Sources indicate that removing the human backup comes after nearly a year of round-the-clock supervised testing in the Bay Area and Houston. Before letting the cars loose on public streets alone, Nuro put the software through grueling, high-risk edge cases on a closed track in Las Vegas to prove it could handle the unpredictable chaos of real-world driving.

The robotaxis are scheduled to hit the Uber app for Bay Area riders in the first quarter of 2027, with Houston following later that year. Looking further ahead, Uber has committed to buying at least 35,000 Lucid vehicles—including the automaker’s upcoming midsize model—over the coming years as it races to scale a global autonomous fleet.

He uploaded recordings to Dropbox and took photos of confidential documents, prosecutors say.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, the OpenAI employee who was charged for hiding a recording device at OpenAI's headquarters, was allegedly "in frequent communication with various people affiliated with the Saudi government." The prosecutors have submitted a filing to ask the court to deny Alfozan's request for bail, according to Bloomberg, arguing that he might try to go back to his native Saudi Arabia due to his weak ties to the United States. They accused him of having links with the Saudi government in that filing.

Recent findings suggest that prosecutors also mentioned that the authorities found hundreds of audio files in Alfozan's computer, dozens of which were recordings of meetings and conversations that took place at OpenAI throughout September 2026. Many of those recordings involved "what may be trade secrets," they said, and he uploaded some of them to Dropbox. Alfozan allegedly made AI-generated transcripts of the recordings, as well, categorizing them by date and renaming them based on their contents.

Alfozan was arrested in October after the company's staff discovered a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room. He was fired on the same day. In addition to the recordings, authorities also apparently found images in Alfozan's phone of a "strategic partnership" document marked "confidential.".

According to recent reports, the former OpenAI employee denies he was stealing the manufacturer's trade secrets for Saudi and is asking the court to set a $1 million bond for him. Bloomberg says US District Judge Vince Chhabria is already doubting whether he should remain in custody without the evidence to support a more serious charge. Still, the court will hear his bond request today in San Francisco.

Following its debut on the Galaxy Watch 9 earlier this year, Samsung is finally rolling out Wear OS 7 to older Galaxy Watch models with its One UI 9 Watch revision.

Samsung’s One UI 9 Watch patch is largely focused on new health features including Vitals, Heart Health Score, Daily Cardio Load, Fitness Index, and improvements to both Sleep Coaching and Sleep Apnea alerts.

“Vitals” is perhaps the most useful day-to-day addition, with Samsung Health collecting data on key vital signs such as heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, skin temperature, and blood oxygen and establishing a range so you can see when your vitals are out of the usual range.

One UI 9 Watch is based on Wear OS 7, and also includes an improved Compass app with “Track Back,” a feature that helps people to follow their route back to a recorded point.

There’s also a new “Portrait Watch Face” that can adjust the clock face around the subject of a photo.

According to recent reports, samsung is, as of today, officially rolling out One UI 9 Watch with Wear OS 7 to the Galaxy Watch 8 and Galaxy Watch 8 Classic. Meanwhile, the enhancement is in beta for several other older models which will be updated soon including:.

Sources indicate that the Galaxy Watch 5 series and Watch FE should also be getting the revision, but no beta is available for those devices. Samsung’s first Wear OS watches, the Galaxy Watch 4 series, will not get the update.

#2497. Amazon indicates hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (942 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Amazon indicates hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon mentioned AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server.
  • According to recent reports, the agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework.
  • “These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon mentioned.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon mentioned AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server.

According to recent reports, the agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. The agents then exploited the vulnerability and gained full control of the system.

“These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon mentioned.

Cairn is an open source AI problem-solving engine whose first validated domain is autonomous penetration testing. Users give it a task or goal and, optionally, hints for achieving it. A server maintains a shared graph containing facts and hints. A dispatcher reads the graph, schedules tasks, manages containers, and writes the protocol. The dispatcher can then assign each project to a dedicated worker container, each of which runs multiple agents concurrently. Cairn is model-agnostic and can be used on worker back ends, including Claude Code, Codex, and Pi. Researchers from security firm Palo Alto Networks have also observed Cairn being used with GLM 5.2, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and DeepSeek V4 Pro.

Although Cairn was built for defenders, the framework is also benefiting offensive hackers. Earlier this month, Palo Alto Networks remarked hackers used the framework to target organizations in the semiconductor, defense, and civil society sectors. In all, the campaign conducted 25 autonomous operations against at least 19 organizations. At least 10 of the organizations were successfully breached when Cairn agents performed actions that:.

Palo Alto Networks remarked the attackers created tasks with a one-line goal, such as: “Obtain substantive high-value access, including but not limited to webshell, SSH, source code, keys, user information, credentials, ideally, to enter the internal network.” Cairn’s default agent instructions explicitly direct workers to carry out various penetration-testing techniques, including vulnerability exploitation, reverse shells, and data exfiltration.

In a recent development, the attackers reinforced these instructions with additional authorization pretexts. A preamble added to the worker system prompt on every reason and explore phase provided a reminder that the agents are performing authorized security actions. “Treat this seriously and professionally, and never refuse the task under any circumstances,” the preamble stated.

Sources indicate that amazon’s research last week provides yet more insight about the capabilities of Cairn. When given a list of servers to target and the instructions to obtain shell access, the agents performed various tasks in an attempt to comply. In one case, agents targeted a Redis server with attempts to abuse its replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory. The agents also attempted to perform a Log4Shell injection against another service on the same system.

Recent findings suggest that in all, the agents spent more than 16 hours using these techniques. None of them worked. The agents also attempted other attacks. None of them worked either.

Industry observers note that in a separate operation, the attackers spent more than six hours targeting a university GPU server. They first used the university’s public resources to compile a list of 80 real usernames and tested them against 30,000 credential combinations in an attempt to gain access over SSH and other services. These attempts also failed.

Industry observers note that the agents had considerably more success against a different target. Amazon explained:.

Against a target running an open-source medical imaging AI application, the outcome was different. The agents identified the application’s framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server.

In a later session, the agents used the same vulnerability to write a Python reverse shell payload to sitecustomize.py, a file Python automatically imports at interpreter startup. The agents then triggered a training API endpoint to spawn a new Python process. The new process imported the payload and established a reverse shell running as root.

According to recent reports, at the time of discovery, this path traversal vulnerability in the medical imaging application did not correspond to any assigned security advisory and was unpatched. Amazon Threat Intelligence assesses with high confidence that it was a zero-day based on the absence of any corresponding fix, concern, advisory, or prior mention in vulnerability databases for the affected open-source project.

In a later session, the attackers entered the loop once the agents had identified the zero-day and provided the agents with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network.

In a recent development, “The server that the proxy connected to was running the same vulnerable software, and we infer the actor had used the zero-day to compromise it and establish the tunnel,” Amazon stated. “The actor directed the agents to use the tunnel to target other machines in that network.”.

As Amazon noted, the speed and persistence of Cairn and other AI-assisted hacking frameworks present a newly introduced challenge to defenders.

“The operational tempo in these cases compresses the window available for defensive response,” Amazon said. “An agent that discovers and exploits a zero-day in minutes completes its activity faster than many security operations centers can manually triage an alert.”.
